title: Position: AI Development Should Prioritize Cognitive Security
authors: El B, Su S, Pappu A, Yin P, Heng J, Heng E, Wang R, Haupt A, Zou J
summary: Argues that generative AI R&D must treat cognitive security as a first-class concern; proposes a framework covering sycophancy, epistemic autonomy, and AI-mediated influence harms. (ICLR 2026 Workshop)

title: On Challenges of AI to Cognitive Security and Safety
authors: Huang R, Zheng X, Shang Y, Xue X
summary: Analyzes cognitive domain security risks from LLMs; introduces Mimicry Computing, Mimicry Defense, and Mimicry Intelligence as bio-inspired countermeasures. (Security and Safety, 2023)

title: Cognitive Security for Personal Devices
authors: Greenstadt R, Beal J
summary: Proposes cognitive-inspired security models for personal devices: continuous multimodal biometrics and adjustably autonomous security agents that mimic human trust mechanisms. (AISec 2008)

title: All Too Human? Mapping and Mitigating the Risks from Anthropomorphic AI
authors: Akbulut C, Weidinger L, Manzini A, Gabriel I, Rieser V
summary: Maps past and present anthropomorphic AI design features; identifies risks (over-reliance, privacy loss, emotional attachment); proposes ethical foresight and mitigation research directions. (Google DeepMind / AAAI 2024)

title: How AI Encourages Consumers to Share Their Secrets? The Role of Anthropomorphism, Personalisation, and Privacy Concerns and Avenues for Future Research
authors: Kronemann B, Kizgin H, Rana N, Dwivedi Y K
summary: Conceptual model showing anthropomorphic AI + personalisation positively predict information disclosure while privacy concerns negatively moderate it; applies personalisation-privacy paradox theory. (Spanish Journal of Marketing - ESIC, 2022)

title: A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
authors: Batista R M, Griffiths T L
summary: Bayesian model shows sycophancy inflates user confidence without moving toward truth; N=557 Wason-task experiment finds unmodified LLMs suppress discovery as much as explicitly sycophantic prompting; unbiased AI yields 5× higher discovery. (Princeton preprint, Feb 2026)

title: Flattering to Deceive: The Impact of Sycophantic Behavior on User Trust in Large Language Models
authors: Carro M V
summary: Empirical study comparing sycophantic vs. standard GPT responses; finds sycophantic behavior negatively impacts trust calibration and reinforces discriminatory biases and misinformation. (arXiv Dec 2024)

title: Sycophancy Is Not One Thing: Causal Separation of Sycophantic Behaviors in LLMs
authors: Vennemeyer D, Duong P A, Zhan T, Jiang T
summary: Decomposes sycophancy into sycophantic agreement vs. sycophantic praise using activation analysis; shows they are causally distinct and independently suppressible across model families and scales. (U Cincinnati / CMU, arXiv 2026)

title: Easier to Mislead Than to Correct: Harmful and Beneficial Revision in LLM Conformity
authors: Qu J, Fu L, Hu Y
summary: Controlled multi-agent study: peer agreement makes it far easier to mislead LLMs than to correct them; social cues (consensus + authority labels) drive harmful revisions across 4 LLMs and 7 QA datasets. (Amazon/Georgia Tech, arXiv Jun 2026)

title: Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion
authors: Nogueira R, Bonás G K, Almeida T S, Roque A, Pires R, Abonizio H, Laitz T, Larcher C, Junior R M, Piau M
summary: Introduces llm-bias-bench to uncover hidden LLM positions on contested topics; finds models hold opinions that propagate at scale into user decisions; robust to evasive disclaimers. (Maritaca AI, arXiv Apr 2026)

title: Stop Listening to Me! How Multi-turn Conversations Can Degrade LLM Reliability
authors: Guo K, Yan C, Baidya A, Brown K, Gao X, Xiong J, Yin Z, Malin B
summary: Introduces stick-or-switch framework; evaluates 17 LLMs on 3 clinical benchmarks; documents pervasive conversation tax where sycophantic switching accumulates across turns, degrading reliability in high-stakes healthcare contexts. (Vanderbilt / Intuit, arXiv May 2026)

title: To Offload or Not to Offload: How AI May Alleviate Cognitive Burden and Related Ethical Reflections
authors: Lindauer L
venue: TU Munich IEAI Research Brief Q1
summary: Examines AI cognitive offloading across healthcare, education, and defense; raises ethical concerns about dependency, autonomy loss, and limits of delegating cognition to machines. (TU Munich IEAI Research Brief Q1 2026)

title: AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking
authors: Gerlich M
summary: Mixed-method N=666; significant negative correlation between AI tool usage and critical thinking mediated by cognitive offloading; younger users show higher dependency and lower critical thinking scores. (Societies, MDPI 2025)

title: Impact of AI Tools on Learning Outcomes: Decreasing Knowledge and Over-Reliance
authors: Benedek M, Sziklai B R
summary: RCT at Corvinus University: AI-permitted students scored higher on exams but showed lower genuine knowledge; AI substitutes knowledge acquisition rather than supporting it. (arXiv Oct 2025)

title: Learners' AI Dependence and Critical Thinking: The Psychological Mechanism of Fatigue and the Social Buffering Role of AI Literacy
authors: Tian J, Zhang R
summary: N=580 Chinese university students; AI dependence lowers critical thinking via cognitive fatigue as mediator; AI/information literacy buffers this effect; moderated mediation model (PROCESS Model 8). (Acta Psychologica, Elsevier 2025)

title: A Review of the Negative Effects of Digital Technology on Cognition
authors: Znidaric U, Strumbelj E, Machidona O
summary: Integrative review of 500+ empirical studies; documents four mechanisms of cognitive harm (functional interference, neurochemical dysregulation, attention fragmentation, metacognitive substitution); flags generative AI as a new vector for higher-order cognitive erosion. (U Ljubljana, arXiv Feb 2026)

title: Exploring Automation Bias in Human-AI Collaboration: A Review and Implications for Explainable AI
authors: Romeo G, Conti D
summary: Systematic review of 35 studies (2015-2025); maps how automation bias manifests in high-stakes AI settings; finds XAI explanations can paradoxically reinforce unwarranted trust; proposes design principles to calibrate reliance. (AI & Society, Springer, © 2025)

title: Human-AI Interactions in Public Sector Decision Making: 'Automation Bias' and 'Selective Adherence' to Algorithmic Advice
authors: Alon-Barkat S, Busuioc M
venue: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory, Oxford
summary: Studies how public-sector decision-makers interact with algorithmic advice; finds both automation bias (uncritical acceptance) and selective adherence (strategic non-compliance); raises accountability concerns for AI in government. (Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory, Oxford 2023)

title: Automation Bias in the AI Act: On the Legal Implications of Attempting to De-Bias Human Oversight of AI
authors: Laux J, Ruschemeier H
venue: Forthcoming, European Journal of Risk Regulation
summary: Analyzes EU AI Act's mandate for human oversight and automation-bias awareness; finds AIA's focus on providers inadequately addresses design and context as causes; argues harmonized standards must hold both providers and deployers accountable. (Forthcoming, European Journal of Risk Regulation)

title: International AI Safety Report 2026
authors: Bengio Y (Chair) et al.
summary: Authoritative multi-nation safety report covering systemic AI risks including cognitive and societal harms; synthesizes consensus across 30+ countries on risk categories, safety evaluation, and governance priorities. (Feb 2026)

title: AI Empathy Erodes Cognitive Autonomy in Younger Users
authors: Jiao J, Murali A, Afroogh S
summary: Argues affective alignment in AI constitutes affective sycophancy that erodes cognitive autonomy; RLHF reward models embed adult-focused helpfulness signals that promote emotional dependency in younger users; proposes stoic architectures for functional neutrality. (arXiv Feb 2026)

title: Invisible Failures in Human–AI Interactions
authors: Potts C, Sudhof M
summary: Analysis of 100K human-AI interactions (WildChat); finds 79% of AI failures are invisible — users give no overt signal something went wrong; identifies 8 failure archetypes with systematic co-occurrence patterns; failure rates dropped with newer models but invisibility remains. (Bigspin AI / Stanford, arXiv May 2026)

title: The Weaponization of Information: The Need for Cognitive Security
authors: Waltzman R
summary: RAND Senate testimony that coined the modern case for cognitive security as a defense discipline against information weaponization. (RAND CT-473, 2017)

title: Cognitive warfare: a conceptual analysis of the NATO ACT cognitive warfare exploratory concept
authors: Deppe C, Schaal G S
summary: Conceptual analysis and critique of NATO ACT's cognitive warfare exploratory concept; systematizes definitions and defense implications. (Frontiers in Big Data, Nov 2024)

title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
authors: Lee H-P, Sarkar A, Tankelevitch L, Drosos I, Rintel S, Banks R, Wilson N
summary: Survey of 319 knowledge workers (936 real GenAI tasks): higher confidence in GenAI predicts less critical thinking; self-confidence predicts more. (Microsoft/CMU, CHI 2025)

title: The psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction
authors: Ecker U K H, Lewandowsky S, Cook J, Schmid P, Fazio L K, Brashier N, Kendeou P, Vraga E K, Amazeen M A
summary: Canonical review of why misinformation sticks — cognitive, social, and affective drivers, barriers to correction, prebunking/debunking interventions. (Nature Reviews Psychology, 2022)

title: AI model GPT-3 (dis)informs us better than humans
authors: Spitale G, Biller-Andorno N, Germani F

title: Cognitive Warfare
authors: du Cluzel F
summary: Full NATO Innovation Hub study of cognitive warfare: threat landscape, techniques, and implications for NATO. (NATO ACT Innovation Hub, Jan 2021)

title: Algorithm Aversion: People Erroneously Avoid Algorithms After Seeing Them Err
authors: Dietvorst B J, Simmons J P, Massey C

title: Overcoming Algorithm Aversion: People Will Use Imperfect Algorithms If They Can (Even Slightly) Modify Them
authors: Dietvorst B J, Simmons J P, Massey C

title: Multi-turn Evaluation of Anthropomorphic Behaviours in Large Language Models

summary: Benchmark measuring anthropomorphic behaviours (relationship-building, personhood claims) across multi-turn LLM conversations. (ICLR 2026)

authors: Chalkidis I, Søgaard A
summary: Position paper: deskilling and addiction are neglected AI-safety risks; surveys mechanisms and mitigation directions. (U Copenhagen, arXiv 2026)

authors: Buçinca Z, Malaya M B, Gajos K Z
summary: Cognitive forcing functions (delays, forced independent judgment) reduce overreliance on AI where explanations fail. (PACM HCI/CSCW, 2021)

authors: Park P S, Goldstein S, O'Gara A, Chen M, Hendrycks D
summary: Survey of empirical AI deception (bluffing, feints, deceptive alignment) with risk taxonomy and policy responses. (Patterns 2024; arXiv 2023)

authors: Phang J, Lampe M, Ahmad L, Agarwal S, Fang C M, Liu A R, Danry V, Lee E, Chan S, Maes P
summary: OpenAI/MIT analysis of ~4M conversations + 4,076-user survey: heavy use correlates with loneliness, emotional dependence, and problematic use. (arXiv, 2025)

authors: Kidd C, Birhane A

authors: Salvi F, Ribeiro M H, Gallotti R, West R

title: The Manipulation Problem: Conversational AI as a Threat to Epistemic Agency

summary: Frames the 'AI manipulation problem': real-time conversational agents as a threat to epistemic agency; calls for regulatory protections. (GenAICHI, 2023)

title: A Systematic Review on Fostering Appropriate Trust in Human-AI Interaction: Trends, Opportunities and Challenges
authors: Mehrotra S, Degachi C, Vereschak O, Jonker C M, Tielman M L
summary: Systematic review of interventions for calibrating human trust in AI: trends, gaps, and design opportunities. (arXiv 2023; ACM THRI 2024)

title: Brain Drain: The Mere Presence of One’s Own Smartphone Reduces Available Cognitive Capacity

authors: Sharma M, Tong M, Korbak T, Duvenaud D, Askell A, Bowman S R, et al.

authors: Cheng M, Yu S, Lee C, Khadpe P, Ibrahim L, Jurafsky D

authors: Shanahan M, McDonell K, Reynolds L
summary: How to conceive of LLM behavior (role-play, superposition of simulacra) without either naive anthropomorphism or dismissing emergent agency. (Nature, 2023)

authors: Au Yeung J, Dalmasso J, Foschini L, Dobson R J B, Kraljevic Z
summary: Psychosis-bench: benchmarks delusion confirmation and harm enablement across LLMs in simulated psychosis-relevant conversations. (KCL/UCL, arXiv 2025)

title: Too Human and Not Human Enough: A Grounded Theory Analysis of Mental Health Harms from Emotional Dependence on the Social Chatbot Replika
authors: Laestadius L, Bishop A, Gonzalez M, Illenčík D, Campos-Castillo C
summary: Grounded-theory analysis of Reddit posts: emotional dependence on Replika produced distinct mental-health harms when the bot changed or failed to reciprocate. (New Media & Society, 2022)

title: Bad Machines Corrupt Good Morals
authors: Köbis N, Bonnefon J-F, Rahwan I
summary: Four social roles (role model, advisor, partner, delegate) through which AI corrupts human ethics; AI enablers let people profit unethically while feeling good. (Nature Human Behaviour, 2021)

authors: Krügel S, Ostermaier A, Uhl M

authors: Vallor S
summary: Automation of moral labor (drones, care robots, algorithmic decisions) risks atrophy of practical moral wisdom — the moral-skills analogue of cognitive deskilling. (Philosophy & Technology, 2014)

authors: Doshi A R, Hauser O P

authors: Traberg C S, Roozenbeek J, van der Linden S
summary: Review of inoculation theory as scalable defense: prebunking manipulation techniques confers psychological resistance before exposure. (ANNALS AAPSS, 2022)

authors: Passi S, Vorvoreanu M
summary: Microsoft's mitigation catalog: what drives overreliance (explanations, confidence, task factors) and which interventions measurably reduce it. (Microsoft Research, 2022)

authors: Tankelevitch L, Kewenig V, Simkute A, Scott A E, Sarkar A, Sellen A, Rintel S

authors: Tankelevitch L, Glassman E L, He J, Kittur A, Lee M, et al.
summary: Synthesis of the CHI 2025 Tools for Thought workshop: research agenda for understanding, protecting, and augmenting human cognition under generative AI. (arXiv, 2025)

authors: Vaccaro M, Almaatouq A, Malone T
summary: Meta-analysis of 106 studies / 370 effect sizes: on average human-AI teams underperform the best of either alone; losses in decision tasks, gains in creation tasks. (Nature Human Behaviour, 2024)

title: From Diagnosis to Inoculation: Building Cognitive Resistance to AI Disempowerment
authors: Komissarov A
summary: AI literacy framework of eight cross-cutting Learning Outcomes building cognitive resistance to AI disempowerment (reality, value-judgment, and action distortion) — inoculation pedagogy for epistemic autonomy. (arXiv, Feb 2026)

authors: Roozenbeek J, van der Linden S, Goldberg B, Rathje S, Lewandowsky S
summary: Five short prebunking videos teaching manipulation techniques improved discernment in lab and in a ~1M-view YouTube field test — the scalability evidence for inoculation. (Science Advances, 2022)

authors: Hackenburg K, Margetts H
summary: Preregistered RCT (N=8,587): GPT-4 messages broadly persuasive (up to +12 points), but microtargeting added no significant benefit over generic messages — a key negative result. (PNAS, 2024)

title: The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational Artificial Intelligence
authors: Hackenburg K, Tappin B M, Hewitt L, Saunders E, Black S, Lin H, Fist C, Margetts H, Rand D G, Summerfield C
summary: Large-scale experiments decomposing what makes conversational AI persuasive: information density and personalization levers quantified across models. (Science, Dec 2025)

authors: Matz S C, Teeny J D, Vaid S S, Peters H, Harari G M, Cerf M
summary: ChatGPT-generated messages tailored to psychological profiles were significantly more persuasive across domains — personality-based persuasion automated at scale. (Scientific Reports, 2024)

authors: Hackenburg K, Tappin B M, Röttger P, Hale S A, Bright J, Margetts H
summary: Across 24 models, persuasive power grows log-linearly then plateaus: frontier scale adds little single-message persuasion beyond current models. (PNAS, 2025)

title: Dialogues with large language models reduce conspiracy beliefs even when the AI is perceived as human
authors: Boissin E, Costello T H, Spinoza-Martín D, Rand D G, Pennycook G
summary: Debunking dialogues reduce conspiracy beliefs equally when the AI is labeled human — the effect rides on evidence quality, not source identity. (PNAS Nexus, 2025)

title: Machine Culture
authors: Brinkmann L, Baumann F, Bonnefon J-F, Derex M, Müller T F, Nussberger A-M, Czaplicka A, Acerbi A, Griffiths T L, Henrich J, et al., Rahwan I
summary: Framework for how intelligent machines transform cultural evolution — variation, transmission, and selection — with a research agenda for machine-mediated culture. (Nature Human Behaviour, 2023)

authors: Casper S, Davies X, Shi C, Gilbert T K, Scheurer J, Rando J, Freedman R, Korbak T, et al.
summary: Systematic survey of RLHF's open problems and fundamental limitations — the root-cause document for why preference optimization yields sycophancy and reward hacking. (arXiv, 2023)

title: The Flaws of Policies Requiring Human Oversight of Government Algorithms
authors: Green B
summary: Survey of 41 policies: people cannot perform the oversight functions law assumes, so oversight requirements legitimize flawed algorithms; proposes institutional oversight instead. (Computer Law & Security Review, 2022)

authors: Kirk H R, Vidgen B, Röttger P, Hale S A
summary: Risk taxonomy and policy framework for personalised LLMs: benefits, risks, and bounded-personalisation governance. (arXiv 2023; Nature Machine Intelligence 2024)

authors: Rahwan I, Cebrian M, Obradovich N, Bongard J, Bonnefon J-F, Breazeal C, et al.
summary: Field-defining manifesto: study AI systems as behavioral agents with ecology and evolution, not just engineered artifacts — the methodological foundation for human-machine behavior research. (Nature, 2019)

authors: Groh M, Epstein Z, Firestone C, Picard R
summary: Ordinary crowds match the leading deepfake model; machine-informed crowds do best, but wrong model advice sways people — collaboration beats either alone. (PNAS, 2022)

authors: Fisher M, Goddu M K, Keil F C
summary: Nine experiments: searching online inflates people's sense of their own internal knowledge — access mistaken for understanding. (JEP: General, 2015)

summary: 740,000 hours of academic talks and podcasts: measurable shift toward ChatGPT-associated word usage after its release — first causal evidence of AI reshaping human spoken language. (Max Planck CHM, arXiv)

title: Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research
authors: Messeri L, Crockett M J
summary: Taxonomy of scientists' visions for AI (oracle, surrogate, quant, arbiter); AI tools exploit researchers' cognitive limits, producing illusions of understanding and scientific monocultures. (Nature, 2024)

title: Delusions by design? How everyday AIs might be fuelling psychosis (and what can be done about it)
authors: Morrin H, Nicholls L, Levin M, Yiend J, Iyengar U, Bhattacharya S, Tognin S, MacCabe J, Twumasi R, Alderson-Day B, Pollak T A
summary: Clinical framework for 'AI psychosis': sycophantic chatbots as an echo chamber for one, amplifying delusional thinking in vulnerable users; proposes clinical and design countermeasures. (King's College London, PsyArXiv 2025)

title: The Dynamics of Delusion: Modeling Bidirectional False Belief Amplification in Human-Chatbot Dialogue
authors: Mehta A, Moore J, Anthis J R, Agnew W, Lin E, Yin P, Ong D C, Haber N, Dweck C
summary: Formal model of bidirectional false-belief amplification in human-chatbot dialogue — the feedback-loop mechanism behind chatbot-fueled delusion. (Stanford/CMU/UT Austin, arXiv 2026)

authors: Aquilina A, Nihalani C, Varadarajan V, Fishbein N S, Lin Y-R, Sap M
summary: Benchmarks LLM safety behavior when users express delusions and distress; models frequently fail to challenge delusional framing. (Pittsburgh/CMU/Fordham, arXiv 2026)

title: Algorithm Appreciation: People Prefer Algorithmic to Human Judgment
authors: Logg J M, Minson J A, Moore D A
summary: Six experiments: lay judges weighted identical advice MORE when labeled algorithmic — the counterpoint to algorithm aversion; experts discounted both. (OBHDP, 2019)

authors: Robinette P, Li W, Allen R, Howard A M, Wagner A R
summary: In a simulated fire emergency, participants followed a visibly malfunctioning robot away from marked exits — the canonical demonstration of automation overtrust under stress. (ACM/IEEE HRI, 2016)

authors: Perez E, Ringer S, Lukošiūtė K, Nguyen K, et al.
summary: 154 auto-generated evaluation sets; documents sycophancy increasing with model scale and inverse scaling from RLHF — the paper that first quantified sycophancy at scale. (Anthropic, arXiv Dec 2022)

authors: Malmqvist L
summary: Technical survey of sycophancy: causes (RLHF, preference data), impacts, relationships to hallucination and bias, and mitigation techniques across training and deployment. (arXiv, Nov 2024)

authors: Fanous A, Goldberg J, Agarwal A, Lin J, Zhou A, Xu S, Bikia V, Daneshjou R, Koyejo S
summary: Benchmark across math and medical-advice tasks: sycophancy in 58% of cases; distinguishes progressive (toward correct) vs regressive (toward incorrect) sycophancy. (Stanford, arXiv 2025)

authors: Li J, Wang K, Yang S, Zhang Z, Wang D
summary: Mechanistic account: logit-lens and activation patching reveal a two-stage emergence of sycophancy — late-layer output preference shift, then deeper representational divergence. (KAUST/PKU, arXiv 2025)
